At 4:17 in the afternoon, the rain stopped.

Not gradually. It simply ended, as if someone had lifted a glass dome from over the town. Water clung to the leaves, to the telephone wires, to the red plastic slide in the park. Every surface shone with the stunned brightness of a newly discovered planet.

Mara stepped outside carrying nothing but a blue cup of tea.

The air smelled of wet pavement and earth. Somewhere nearby, a child laughed. A bird, confused by the sudden silence, began a song and abandoned it after three notes.

Across the street, an old man was sweeping his front steps. He had been doing this every day for as long as Mara could remember, though the steps never seemed to grow cleaner. Today he paused and looked up at the sky.

“Beautiful,” he said.

Mara followed his gaze. The clouds were breaking apart, revealing a narrow strip of gold where the sun had begun to set.

“Yes,” she said.

They stood there together, strangers joined by the ordinary miracle of weather.

Then the old man resumed sweeping. Mara took a sip of tea. It had gone cold, but she drank it anyway.

Some moments do not ask to be kept. They arrive, shine briefly, and pass through you—leaving behind no proof except the strange feeling that, for a little while, the world had remembered your name.
